title: Idleness is the enemy (ch. 48)
hook: pray and work, balanced through the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing before the work of God: when the bell rings, the hoe goes down. Your line was nothing before prayer. Did you manage to stop in the middle? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

Three short Latin words: ora et labora. Pray and work. Some people use them to sum up a Benedictine life in a breath. After yesterday, it might seem the monks did nothing but drop their tools and run to chapel. They didn't. The same Rule that puts nothing before prayer also hands every monk a job, and it starts its chapter on daily work with a blunt sentence about what happens to a soul with nothing to do. Today: ora et labora.
screen: `ORA ET LABORA. PRAY AND WORK.` → `NOT ONLY RUNNING TO CHAPEL.` → `EVERY MONK HAS A JOB.`

segments.voice: Chapter forty-eight opens: idleness is the enemy of the soul. So, Benedict says, the brothers should be busy at set times with the work of their hands, and at other set times with holy reading. Tomorrow is the reading. Today is the work. Benedict means real work: the kitchen, the garden, the fields, the workshop. And he doesn't treat it as a lesser thing tolerated between prayers. He says that when monks live by the labor of their hands, as the fathers and the apostles did, then they are truly monks. Work isn't a break from the spiritual life. It's part of it. But the Rule also guards against the opposite trouble. Everything, Benedict says, should be done with measure, for the sake of the fainthearted. The brothers who are weak or delicate get work suited to them, so they're neither idle nor crushed. Not too little, not too much. So the motto isn't really two separate commands. It's a rhythm. Pray, then work, then pray, the day swinging between the two like a gate on a hinge. Prayer keeps work from swallowing the whole person. Work keeps prayer from floating off into daydreams. Ora et labora is a summary people use for that rhythm; the Rule's own sentence is the one about idleness. Look back at the week and it all fits together. The toolbox of good works. Obedience without grumbling. Fewer words. The ladder you climb by stepping down. The seven hours. Nothing before the work of God. And now the work itself, done with the same heart. One house, one rhythm, from the chapel to the bean rows.
screen: `IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.` · `BY THE LABOR OF THEIR HANDS.` · `WITH MEASURE, FOR THE FAINTHEARTED.` · `A RHYTHM, LIKE A GATE ON A HINGE.` · then, large: `ORA ET LABORA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: alternate work and prayer. Settle, and breathe. Lay out the rest of today in your mind as a row of blocks: this job, then that one, then the next. Now picture a small hinge between each block. Thirty seconds, a minute at most. At each hinge, you'll stop, take a breath, and turn toward God, or toward stillness, before the next block starts. Then let the work begin again, done with your whole attention. Notice which block you most want to rush through, and plan a hinge right after it. If you pray, you can make each hinge a short prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Ora et labora. Pray and work: the Benedictine rhythm in three words, with idleness as the enemy and measure as the rule. Today's word.

Your line: pray and work. Today, put a hinge between your jobs: a breath or a short prayer between one task and the next, so the day swings instead of blurs. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns divide their day between the hours of prayer, manual or other work, and sacred reading, and some monasteries support themselves through farming, crafts, teaching or guesthouses.

fork.setup: you're the abbot. one brother is frail and can't keep up in the fields. what does chapter forty-eight ask?
options: excuse him from all work so he can rest.
give him work suited to him, so he's neither idle nor crushed.
keep him in the fields: work is work.
fork.reveal: Benedict wants measure: the weak get suitable work, because idleness is the enemy, and so is a load that breaks them.
